plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.

demo_steps.narration: The crystal lattice contains multiple sets of parallel planes. This face-parallel plane cuts squarely through a single layer of atoms.

demo_steps.title: Diagonal plane
demo_steps.narration: A single crystal also contains diagonal planes. This family intersects atoms across the cube's volume at a different angle.

demo_steps.title: Plane spacing
demo_steps.narration: Moving to an adjacent parallel plane reveals the plane spacing. Notice that the perpendicular spacing between diagonal planes is smaller than between face-parallel planes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Lattice: 27 spheres (radius ~0.12 units, red #d93838) at all coordinate combinations of x, y, z ∈ {-1, 0, 1}. Wireframe: Thin black lines connecting adjacent spheres along the grid axes. Plane: Translucent teal #8bc5c8, double-sided, opacity 0.55. Plane mapping sets an offset value v = (planePosition - 2), so v ∈ {-1, 0, 1}. If 'Face-parallel': plane is perpendicular to the Z-axis at z = v, sized 2.4 × 2.4. If 'Diagonal': plane equation is y - x = v, parallel to the Z-axis, with normal (-0.707, 0.707, 0). The diagonal plane spans z from -1.2 to 1.2, with a width sufficient to reach the ±1.2 bounds of the lattice (e.g., width 3.4 for v=0, and ~1.7 for v=±1).
interactionPlan.notes: Ensure material transparent: true, depthWrite: false for the teal plane so the internal atoms and lines render correctly through it. Rebuild or adjust the plane's position, rotation, and scale reactively when the toggle or slider changes.

authoredContext:
Although the figure depicts a crystal as a two-dimensional array of scattering centers for simplicity, real crystals are structures in three dimensions. Scattering can occur simultaneously from different families of planes at different orientations and spacing patterns known as called Bragg planes, as shown in the figure. The resulting interference pattern can be quite complex.

Because of the regularity that makes a crystal structure, one crystal can have many families of planes within its geometry, each one giving rise to X-ray diffraction.

Figure shows two crystal lattices, with atoms shown as small circles, connected to each other by lines. In the first lattice, flat planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In the second, slanted planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In each case, the planes are seen as a combination of different atoms in the same lattice.
